_comment: Hand-written Games in the other Modes for the demo Graph Algorithms Module, built on the pages of graph-algorithms.json. Each list uses its Mode's Gemini response shape and must pass that Mode's generation checks (npm run db:seed -- --check). Apogee reuses graph-algorithms.json's Dive Prompts.

prompts.text: Which data structure does BFS use to decide which vertex to visit next?
prompts.explanation: BFS takes the vertex at the front of a queue and adds its unvisited neighbors to the back, so it explores level by level.
prompts.evidence_quote: It uses a queue: take the vertex at the front, then add its unvisited neighbors to the back.

prompts.text: Which algorithm finds single-source shortest paths and still works with negative edge weights?
prompts.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge V - 1 times, which stays correct with negative edge weights; Dijkstra breaks on them.
prompts.evidence_quote: Finds shortest paths from one source, and works with negative edge weights.

prompts.text: What is the running time of Floyd-Warshall?
prompts.explanation: Floyd-Warshall runs a dynamic program over a V x V table once for each of the V intermediate vertices.
prompts.evidence_quote: Running time: O(V^3).

prompts.text: Which algorithm finds every strongly connected component in a single DFS using low-link values?
prompts.explanation: Tarjan's algorithm needs one DFS with low-link values and a stack; Kosaraju's needs two passes.
prompts.evidence_quote: Tarjan's algorithm finds every SCC in a single DFS, using low-link values and a stack.

prompts.text: How many times does Bellman-Ford relax every edge?
prompts.explanation: A shortest path has at most V - 1 edges, so V - 1 rounds of relaxing every edge are enough.
prompts.evidence_quote: Relaxes every edge V - 1 times.

prompts.text: When does a topological sort of a graph exist?
options: When it has no directed cycle
When its edge weights are non-negative
prompts.correct_option: When it has no directed cycle
prompts.explanation: A topological order needs every edge to point forward, which is impossible around a directed cycle.
prompts.evidence_quote: It only exists when the graph has no directed cycle.

prompts.text: Which structure does Kruskal's algorithm use to check whether an edge would create a cycle?
prompts.explanation: Union-find tracks which vertices are already in the same component, so an edge inside one component would close a cycle.
prompts.evidence_quote: Kruskal uses union-find to check whether an edge would create a cycle.

prompts.text: How much space does an adjacency list use?
prompts.explanation: Each vertex stores only its own neighbors, so the space grows with the vertices plus the edges; a matrix needs O(V^2).
prompts.evidence_quote: Adjacency list: each vertex stores a list of its neighbors. Uses O(V + E) space.

prompts.text: Which algorithm finds a maximum matching in a bipartite graph in O(E sqrt(V)) time?
prompts.explanation: Hopcroft-Karp beats the basic augmenting path method, which takes O(V * E).
prompts.evidence_quote: Hopcroft-Karp finds a maximum matching in a bipartite graph faster than the basic augmenting path method: O(E sqrt(V)).

prompts.text: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm break on graphs with negative edge weights?
options: It only works on unweighted graphs
It relaxes each edge just V - 1 times
It assumes a settled node can't get a shorter path later
It needs a graph with no directed cycle
prompts.correct_option: It assumes a settled node can't get a shorter path later
prompts.explanation: With a negative edge, a shorter path to an already settled node can appear later, and Dijkstra never revisits it.
prompts.evidence_quote: Dijkstra breaks on graphs that have negative edge weights: once a node is settled, it assumes no shorter path to it can appear later.

prompts.text: Which minimum spanning tree algorithm grows one tree outward from a start vertex?
prompts.explanation: Prim's algorithm always adds the cheapest edge leaving its single growing tree; Kruskal's joins many pieces.
prompts.evidence_quote: Prim's algorithm grows one tree from a start vertex, always adding the cheapest edge that leaves the tree.

prompts.text: What does DFS use to go as deep as possible before backtracking?
prompts.explanation: DFS keeps its path on a stack, either an explicit one or the call stack when written recursively.
prompts.evidence_quote: It uses a stack, or recursion, which uses the call stack.

prompts.text: On an unweighted graph, which algorithm finds the shortest path with the fewest edges?
prompts.explanation: BFS reaches vertices in order of how many edges away they are, so the first time it reaches a vertex is by a shortest path.
prompts.evidence_quote: On an unweighted graph, BFS finds the shortest path (fewest edges) from the source to every vertex.

prompts.text: Which data structure does Dijkstra's algorithm use to pick the next node?
prompts.explanation: Dijkstra always takes the unvisited node with the smallest known distance, which a min-heap returns quickly.
prompts.evidence_quote: Uses a priority queue (min-heap).

prompts.text: Traversal that explores a graph level by level, using a queue

answers.evidence_quote: BFS visits every neighbor at the current depth before moving one level deeper.

prompts.explanation: On an unweighted graph it also finds the shortest path (fewest edges).

prompts.text: Traversal that goes as far down one branch as possible before backtracking

answers.evidence_quote: DFS explores as far down one branch as possible before backtracking.

prompts.explanation: It is the building block for cycle detection, topological sort and SCCs.

prompts.text: A linear ordering of a DAG's vertices in which every edge points forward

answers.evidence_quote: A topological sort is a linear ordering of the vertices of a DAG such that for every edge (u, v), u comes before v.

prompts.explanation: One way to get it: run DFS and list vertices in reverse order of finishing time.

prompts.text: A directed graph that contains no cycles

answers.evidence_quote: A DAG is a directed acyclic graph: a directed graph with no cycles.

prompts.explanation: Only these graphs have a topological order.

prompts.text: Single-source shortest paths with a min-heap, for non-negative edge weights only

answers.evidence_quote: Finds shortest paths from one source in a graph with non-negative edge weights.

prompts.explanation: It runs in O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap.

prompts.text: Single-source shortest paths that relaxes every edge V - 1 times and copes with negative weights

answers.evidence_quote: Finds shortest paths from one source, and works with negative edge weights.

prompts.explanation: One more pass over the edges detects a negative cycle.

prompts.text: Dynamic program that finds the shortest path between every pair of vertices

answers.evidence_quote: Finds the shortest paths between every pair of vertices (all-pairs shortest paths).

prompts.explanation: It runs in O(V^3) and handles negative edges but not negative cycles.

prompts.text: Edges that connect every vertex of a weighted, undirected graph with the least total weight

answers.evidence_quote: A minimum spanning tree connects every vertex of a weighted, undirected graph using the least total edge weight.

prompts.explanation: Kruskal, Prim and Borůvka all build one.

prompts.text: Adds edges from cheapest to most expensive, skipping any edge that would close a cycle

answers.evidence_quote: Kruskal's algorithm adds edges from cheapest to most expensive, skipping any edge that would create a cycle

prompts.explanation: It stops once the tree has V - 1 edges, and uses union-find to spot cycles.

prompts.text: Grows a single tree from a start vertex, always taking the cheapest edge leaving it

answers.evidence_quote: Prim's algorithm grows one tree from a start vertex, always adding the cheapest edge that leaves the tree.

prompts.explanation: Unlike Kruskal's, it only ever has one tree.

prompts.text: Structure that tracks which vertices are already in the same component

answers.evidence_quote: Keeps track of which vertices are already in the same component.

prompts.explanation: With union by rank and path compression, each operation is almost O(1).

prompts.text: A maximal set of vertices in which every vertex can reach every other one

answers.evidence_quote: An SCC is a maximal set of vertices in which every vertex can reach every other vertex.

prompts.explanation: Kosaraju's and Tarjan's algorithms find them in O(V + E).

prompts.text: Runs DFS twice, the second time on the graph with every edge reversed

answers.evidence_quote: Kosaraju's algorithm runs DFS to get finishing times, reverses every edge, then runs DFS again in decreasing finishing time.

prompts.explanation: Each tree in the second pass is one strongly connected component.

prompts.text: Finds a maximum bipartite matching faster than the basic augmenting path method

answers.evidence_quote: Hopcroft-Karp finds a maximum matching in a bipartite graph faster than the basic augmenting path method

prompts.explanation: It runs in O(E sqrt(V)).

prompts.text: A set of edges in which no two edges share a vertex

answers.evidence_quote: A matching is a set of edges in which no two edges share a vertex.

prompts.explanation: Augmenting paths grow a matching one edge at a time.

prompts.text: A V x V table recording the edge between each pair of vertices

answers.evidence_quote: Adjacency matrix: a V x V table where entry (u, v) records the edge from u to v.

prompts.explanation: It uses O(V^2) space, more than an adjacency list's O(V + E).
